title: Robustness and Limitations
text: The closed-form results on The Model are exact for one assumed transition matrix. This page asks where a control change has the most leverage, how much the results move when the transition probabilities are uncertain, and whether the solver code is correct. It ends with the model’s limitations and the data a calibrated version would need.

title: Robustness and Limitations
text:
One-Row-at-a-Time Control Sensitivity
To ask where a control change has the most leverage, the comparison must change one row at a time and hold the starting stage fixed. Starting from S1 (so every row lies on the attacker’s path), the analysis applies two changes to each row separately: (a) a standardized shift of 0.05 of probability from the row’s largest non-self, non-A1 edge to A1, and (b) replacing that row with its improved-posture row.


Display code
harden_one_row <- function(P, i, delta = 0.05) {
  donor <- unname(which.max(replace(P[i, ], c(i, 7), 0)))
  P[i, donor] <- P[i, donor] - delta
  P[i, 7] <- P[i, 7] + delta
  list(P = P, donor = all_state_names[donor])
}

outcomes_from_s1 <- function(P) {
  B <- solve_absorbing_markov(P[1:t_dim, 1:t_dim], P[1:t_dim, 7:9], step_hours)$B
  c(cont = B[1, 1], cat = B[1, 2] + B[1, 3])
}
shift_delta <- params$sensitivity$shift_delta$value
prop_rel <- params$sensitivity$prop_rel$value
seed <- params$seed$value

base_s1 <- outcomes_from_s1(P_baseline_raw)

sens_df <- map(seq_len(t_dim), \(i) {
  shifted <- harden_one_row(P_baseline_raw, i, delta = shift_delta)
  full_row <- P_baseline_raw
  full_row[i, ] <- P_hardened_raw[i, ]

  tibble(
    Stage = transient_names[i],
    Donor_Edge = str_extract(shifted$donor, "^[SA][0-9]"),
    Shift_Cont = outcomes_from_s1(shifted$P)["cont"] - base_s1["cont"],
    Shift_Cat = outcomes_from_s1(shifted$P)["cat"] - base_s1["cat"],
    Row_Cont = outcomes_from_s1(full_row)["cont"] - base_s1["cont"],
    Row_Cat = outcomes_from_s1(full_row)["cat"] - base_s1["cat"]

}) |>
  list_rbind()

How to read the table. Each row tests one change to the defenses at a single stage, holding everything else fixed, for attacks that start at S1. The first approach moves a fixed 0.05 of probability from the attacker’s most likely next move to containment; the donor column names that move. The second swaps in that stage’s improved-posture values. Each column shows the resulting change in containment or catastrophe, in percentage points; positive containment changes are gains.
What the table tells you. Under the fixed shift, improving S2 gives the largest containment gain, 2.25 points, against 2.12 for S1, and the gains shrink for deeper stages. Early-stage defenses therefore carry somewhat more leverage, but the differences are modest, and the checks further down this page show that the order of S1 and S2 is not reliable. The values come from assumed inputs, not measured control effects.
In more detail
Under these illustrative parameters, the largest standardized containment gain from S1 comes from changing the S2: Initial Foothold row (2.25 pp), not S1 itself (2.12 pp). Gains decline for deeper rows, to 1.43 pp at S6, which is 36% below the best row. Under this standardized shift the gradient looks moderate (the best row is about 1.6 times the last). The next table shows that this depends on how the perturbation is defined, and the ranking check in Parameter Uncertainty shows that the order of the top two rows is not stable. Two caveats: the 0.05 shift is a different relative change in each row, and the table only covers attacks that start at S1. The ranking reflects the hand-set parameters.
Why the ranking looks this way. For a small shift \(\varepsilon\) from edge \((i, j)\) to A1, the change in containment from S1 is approximately
\[\Delta B_{1,A1} \approx \varepsilon \, N_{1i} \, \bigl(1 - B_{j,A1}\bigr)\]
That is, expected visits to row \(i\) times the catastrophic share of the donor state \(j\). The table below confirms that the identity reproduces the standardized-shift column. The modest gradient is the product of two opposing trends: visits fall with depth while the donor’s catastrophic share rises. It also depends on the perturbation design.


Display code
harden_one_row_prop <- function(P, i, rel = 0.10) {
  inc <- rel * P[i, t_dim + 1]
  others <- setdiff(which(P[i, ] > 0), c(i, t_dim + 1))
  P[i, others] <- P[i, others] - inc * P[i, others] / sum(P[i, others])
  P[i, t_dim + 1] <- P[i, t_dim + 1] + inc
  P
}

How to read the table. Each row is one stage whose defenses are improved, for attacks starting at S1. Expected visits is how often an attack passes through that stage on average. The donor share is the chance that an attack at the stage it would otherwise have moved to ends in catastrophe. Multiplying the two by the 0.05 shift gives a predicted gain, shown next to the actual gain. The last column repeats the exercise with a 10% proportional improvement instead.
What the table tells you. The prediction matches the actual gain in every row, so the ranking is explained by two opposing forces: early stages are visited more often, but attacks moving on from them are less likely to end badly. Because these roughly offset, the gains differ only modestly. Under a proportional improvement, the gap between the first and last stages grows from about 1.6 times to 4.0 times, so the answer depends on how an improvement is defined.
The gradient depends on the perturbation. Under a proportional perturbation (+10% relative A1 probability, taken pro rata from the other exits), the upstream-to-downstream ratio is about 4.0× rather than 1.6×. A defensible ranking needs a control-to-parameter mapping, ideally expressed as hazard ratios on rates. A fixed absolute shift is not enough.

title: Robustness and Limitations
text:
Parameter Uncertainty (Dirichlet)
Closed-form results are exact only given \(P\), and \(P\) is uncertain. To quantify that, each transient row is treated as Dirichlet(\(\alpha \cdot p_{\text{row}}\)) over its non-zero entries (structural zeros stay zero), with concentration \(\alpha = 50\) as a stand-in for “moderate confidence” in the elicited values. The solver is re-run on 5,000 sampled matrices per regime.


Display code
draw_P <- function(P, alpha) {
  for (i in seq_len(t_dim)) {
    idx <- which(P[i, ] > 0)
    g <- rgamma(length(idx), shape = alpha * P[i, idx])
    P[i, idx] <- g / sum(g)
  }
  P
}

summarise_draw <- function(P) {
  sol <- solve_absorbing_markov(P[1:t_dim, 1:t_dim], P[1:t_dim, 7:9], step_hours)
  tibble(Stage = transient_names, cont = sol$B[, 1], cat = sol$B[, 2] + sol$B[, 3], hours = sol$hours)
}
alpha_conc <- params$dirichlet$alpha_conc$value
n_draws <- params$dirichlet$n_draws$value

set.seed(seed)
draws <- map(seq_len(n_draws), \(d) {
  b <- summarise_draw(draw_P(P_baseline_raw, alpha_conc))
  h <- summarise_draw(draw_P(P_hardened_raw, alpha_conc))
  tibble(draw = d, Stage = b$Stage,
         cont_b = b$cont, cat_b = b$cat, hours_b = b$hours,
         cont_h = h$cont, cat_h = h$cat, hours_h = h$hours)
}) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  mutate(Stage = factor(Stage, levels = transient_names))

q05 <- \(x) quantile(x, 0.05)
q95 <- \(x) quantile(x, 0.95)

unc_summary <- draws |>
  summarise(
    cont_b_lo = q05(cont_b), cont_b_hi = q95(cont_b),
    cat_b_lo = q05(cat_b), cat_b_hi = q95(cat_b),
    hours_b_lo = q05(hours_b), hours_b_hi = q95(hours_b),
    p_improved_better = mean(cont_h > cont_b),
    .by = Stage
  ) |>
  left_join(res |> select(Stage = stage, cont_b, cat_b, hours_b) |> mutate(Stage = factor(Stage, levels = transient_names)),
            by = "Stage") |>
  arrange(Stage)

crossing_dist <- draws |>
  summarise(
    cross = which(cat_b > cont_b)[1],
    .by = draw
  ) |>
  count(cross) |>
  mutate(share = n / sum(n))

p_cross_s3 <- crossing_dist |> filter(cross == 3) |> pull(share)

How to read the table. Each row is a starting stage under the baseline. Each cell gives the model’s point estimate followed, in brackets, by a 90% range: the band within which the result fell in 90% of 5,000 reruns with randomly varied input probabilities. Wider ranges mean the result is more sensitive to the assumed inputs. The last column is the share of reruns in which the improved posture contained more attacks than the baseline.
What the table tells you. Uncertainty in the inputs matters. At S3 the chance of catastrophe is 52.9%, but its 90% range runs from 42.3% to 63.5%, so whether catastrophe or containment is more likely at S3 can flip. The improved posture beats the baseline in nearly every rerun, but that check is weak by design, because its matrix was built to be better. The ranges also depend on an assumed confidence level, examined next.
The improved-posture comparison draws baseline and improved matrices independently, so the last column checks whether the improvement survives parameter noise, not a paired control effect. The paired comparison below estimates the scenario effect directly.
In more detail
The S3 crossing is fairly, not fully, stable. In 63.7% of draws, catastrophic outcomes first become more likely than containment at S3 (the baseline point estimate); the remaining draws place the crossing at other stages (shares: S2 2.6%; S3 63.7%; S4 32.8%; S5 1.0%). The statement “S3 is the tipping point” is therefore conditional on these parameters and on the assumed concentration \(\alpha\); the α sweep below shows that α changes the location of the crossing, not just the interval widths.
Uncertainty is substantial for the point estimates. At S3 the 90% interval for catastrophic probability is 42.3% to 63.5%, around the point estimate of 52.9%.
The improved posture is better in almost every draw, which says little by itself. The improved posture has higher containment than the baseline in at least 99.9% of draws at every stage. The improved matrix was built to have higher A1 probabilities, and the two regimes are drawn independently, so this check is weak. The paired comparison below gives the size of the difference with an interval.

How to read the table. Each row assumes a different level of confidence in the input probabilities, written α: a low α means the inputs could be well off, and a high α means they are close to right. For each level, the model was rerun 2,000 times. The columns give the share of reruns in which S3 is the first stage where catastrophe is more likely than containment, and the 90% range of the S3 catastrophe probability.
What the table tells you. How sure one can be that S3 is the tipping point depends heavily on how much the inputs are trusted. With low confidence, S3 is the tipping point in only 38.0% of reruns; with high confidence, in 79.1%. The confidence level is itself an assumption, so it should be set from structured expert input rather than chosen for convenience. Until then, the tipping point is best described as around S3, not exactly at S3.
The tipping point depends on α. The share of draws in which the first crossing is at S3 ranges from 38.0% at α = 10 to 79.1% at α = 200. α changes the conclusion, not just the interval width. It should be elicited (for example, by matching expert quantiles for each edge) rather than assumed.


Correlated Detection Quality Across Stages


Display code
shared_sd_log <- params$dirichlet$shared_sd_log$value
set.seed(seed)
shared_cat_s1 <- map_dbl(seq_len(n_draws), \(d) {
  P <- draw_P(P_baseline_raw, alpha_conc)
  f <- exp(rnorm(1, 0, shared_sd_log))
  for (i in seq_len(t_dim)) {
    a_new <- min(P[i, t_dim + 1] * f, 0.95)
    others <- setdiff(seq_len(ncol(P)), t_dim + 1)
    P[i, others] <- P[i, others] * (1 - a_new) / (1 - P[i, t_dim + 1])
    P[i, t_dim + 1] <- a_new
  }
  stopifnot(abs(sum(P[1:t_dim, ]) - t_dim) < 1e-8)
  outcomes_from_s1(P)["cat"]
})
indep_cat_s1 <- draws |> filter(Stage == transient_names[1]) |> pull(cat_b)
shared_int <- quantile(shared_cat_s1, c(0.05, 0.95))
indep_int <- quantile(indep_cat_s1, c(0.05, 0.95))


Correlated detection quality widens the intervals. The analysis above draws each row independently, which lets errors cancel along the attack path. Detection quality is an organizational capability: a SOC that is weak at S2 is probably weak at S3 and S4 too. Multiplying every row’s A1 probability by a common log-normal factor (log-scale SD 0.35) widens the 90% interval for catastrophic probability from S1 from 19.8%–36.0% to 7.0%–51.3%.


Paired Improvement Effect


Display code
# Common random numbers: the same uniforms drive both regimes' gamma draws
draw_pair <- function(Pb, Ph, alpha) {
  for (i in seq_len(t_dim)) {
    idx <- which(Pb[i, ] > 0 | Ph[i, ] > 0)
    u <- runif(length(idx))
    gb <- qgamma(u, shape = pmax(alpha * Pb[i, idx], 1e-8))
    gh <- qgamma(u, shape = pmax(alpha * Ph[i, idx], 1e-8))
    Pb[i, idx] <- gb / sum(gb)
    Ph[i, idx] <- gh / sum(gh)
  }
  list(b = Pb, h = Ph)
}
set.seed(seed)
paired <- map(seq_len(n_draws), \(d) {
  pr <- draw_pair(P_baseline_raw, P_hardened_raw, alpha_conc)
  tibble(draw = d, Stage = transient_names,
         uplift = summarise_draw(pr$h)$cont - summarise_draw(pr$b)$cont)
}) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  mutate(Stage = factor(Stage, levels = transient_names))

paired_summary <- paired |>
  summarise(med = median(uplift), lo = quantile(uplift, 0.05), hi = quantile(uplift, 0.95), .by = Stage) |>

Both postures share the same random variation in each rerun, so the difference reflects the change in posture rather than noise. What the table tells you. The gain is large and clearly positive everywhere: from S1, a median of 24.6 pp, with 90% of reruns between 18.2 pp and 31.7 pp. It is largest for attacks starting at S4. Even so, both postures are hand-set scenarios, not measured controls, so this shows how much difference such a change in assumptions makes, not what a specific security investment would deliver.
The scenario effect has a meaningful interval. Drawing both regimes from the same random numbers (common random numbers through the gamma quantile function) isolates the scenario difference from parameter noise. The S1 containment uplift is 24.6 pp, with a 90% interval of 18.2 pp–31.7 pp. This is still a difference between two hand-set matrices, not a measured control effect.


Robustness of the One-Row Ranking


Display code
shift_cont_from_s1 <- function(P, i, delta = 0.05) {
  donor <- unname(which.max(replace(P[i, ], c(i, t_dim + 1), 0)))
  if (P[i, donor] < delta) return(NA_real_)
  P2 <- P
  P2[i, donor] <- P2[i, donor] - delta
  P2[i, t_dim + 1] <- P2[i, t_dim + 1] + delta
  outcomes_from_s1(P2)["cont"] - outcomes_from_s1(P)["cont"]
}
n_rank <- params$dirichlet$n_rank$value
set.seed(seed)
rank_draws <- map(seq_len(n_rank), \(d) {
  P <- draw_P(P_baseline_raw, alpha_conc)
  g <- map_dbl(seq_len(t_dim), \(i) shift_cont_from_s1(P, i, delta = shift_delta))
  tibble(draw = d, best = which.max(g), s2_beats_s1 = g[2] > g[1])
}) |> list_rbind()

best_row_share <- rank_draws |> count(best) |> mutate(share = n / sum(n))
p_best_s2 <- sum(best_row_share$share[best_row_share$best == 2])
p_best_s1 <- sum(best_row_share$share[best_row_share$best == 1])
p_s2_beats_s1 <- mean(rank_draws$s2_beats_s1, na.rm = TRUE)

section: Simulation Check of the Closed-Form Solver
text:
Simulation Check of the Closed-Form Solver
A short Monte Carlo run from S1 under the baseline matrix is a code-correctness check on \(B\), \(\mathbf{t}\), the conditional times to each outcome, and one cumulative-incidence point. Each simulated value must fall within four Monte Carlo standard errors of its closed-form counterpart.


Display code
simulate_walk <- function(P, start) {
  s <- start
  steps <- 0
  while (s <= t_dim) {
    s <- sample.int(ncol(P), 1, prob = P[s, ])
    steps <- steps + 1
  }
  c(outcome = s - t_dim, steps = steps)
}
n_sim <- params$simulation$n_sim$value
set.seed(seed)
sims <- map(seq_len(n_sim), \(k) simulate_walk(P_baseline_raw, 1)) |>
  map(\(v) tibble(outcome = v[["outcome"]], steps = v[["steps"]])) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  mutate(hours = steps * unname(step_hours[1]))

sim_props <- as.vector(prop.table(table(factor(sims$outcome, levels = 1:3))))

  Quantity = c(absorbing_names, "Expected steps from S1",
               "E[hours | contained], from S1", "E[hours | catastrophic], from S1",
               "P(catastrophic within 24 h), from S1"),
  Closed_form = c(base_solution$B[1, ], base_solution$steps[1],
                  res$t_cont_b[1], res$t_cat_b[1], p_cat_by_24h),
  Simulated = c(sim_props, mean(sims$steps),
                mean(sims$hours[sims$outcome == 1]), mean(sims$hours[sims$outcome > 1]),
                mean(sims$outcome > 1 & sims$hours <= 24)),
  MC_SE = c(sqrt(base_solution$B[1, ] * (1 - base_solution$B[1, ]) / n_sim),
            sd(sims$steps) / sqrt(n_sim),

title: Robustness and Limitations
text:
Limitations and Future Work
The model’s structural assumptions are listed under Parameterization and Assumptions, and the sections above show how sensitive the results are to the elicited inputs. This section covers the data a richer, calibrated version would need.

Future work: real-world data sources
The current model uses none of the following sources. They describe network and identity topology, which tells a richer model which edges exist. They do not by themselves supply the transition probabilities or timing this model needs (see the calibration note after the table).
Network Telemetry & Flow Logs: Real connection edges and service dependencies come from VPC Flow Logs (AWS/Azure/GCP), Zeek/Corelight network analysis sensors, and NetFlow/IPFIX from core network routers and firewalls.
Service Dependency & Configuration Management Databases (CMDB): Service-to-service call maps are extracted from application performance monitoring tools (e.g., Datadog, Dynatrace), service mesh registries (e.g., Istio, Envoy), and enterprise CMDBs (e.g., ServiceNow).
Vulnerability Management & Posture Assessment Scanners: CVSS scores, exploit metrics, and missing patches are pulled via API from enterprise vulnerability scanners such as Tenable Nessus, Qualys, Rapid7 InsightVM, or cloud posture platforms (Wiz, Prisma Cloud).
Active Directory & Identity Access Graphs: Identity edges and lateral movement pathways are exported from tools like BloodHound Enterprise, Microsoft Entra ID, and Okta Access Graph logs.

What the table tells you. Building an accurate map of a real network is a substantial engineering project in its own right. Service dependencies and reconciling names across systems are rated hardest, because records are incomplete and constantly changing. Even with all of this data in hand, the model would still need timestamped incident histories to estimate how likely and how fast each move is, as the calibration notes below explain.


Calibration Data and Survival-Analysis Pitfalls
The parameters of this model are stage-transition probabilities and stage durations. Estimating them requires timestamped transitions rather than topology:

Internal incident-response timelines and EDR or SIEM alert timestamps mapped to MITRE ATT&CK tactics.
Purple-team and breach-and-attack-simulation results (time to detect per technique).
The VERIS Community Database, whose timeline fields record initial compromise, exfiltration, discovery, and containment in coarse units (VERIS Framework).
Public benchmarks as priors: M-Trends, the Sophos Active Adversary Report, and CrowdStrike breakout times.

Fitting these data raises standard survival-analysis issues:

Right censoring: incidents still open at data extraction.
Interval censoring: stage entry is known only to a window, or to a unit such as “days.”
Left truncation and detection-dependent selection: only detected intrusions are recorded.
Competing risks: containment censors progression, so naive Kaplan–Meier estimates of time to catastrophe are biased, and Aalen–Johansen estimators are appropriate.
Unobserved heterogeneity: attacker types differ, for example fast eCrime affiliates versus slow espionage actors.

Multi-state packages such as msm, mstate, and flexsurv handle these directly.

title: Multi-Stage Attack Graph Simulation Via Markov Chains
text:
Enterprise cyber defenses have traditionally relied on static checklists and subjective risk heatmaps that do not capture how adversaries maneuver through networks over time. When advanced persistent threats (APTs) or ransomware operators infiltrate an organization, they do not execute a single isolated attack; they work through a sequence of tactical stages, from initial delivery to privilege escalation and lateral movement. Traditional security metrics rarely quantify the speed of this progression or the likelihood of catastrophic outcomes relative to early containment.
This project implements a multi-stage cyber attack simulator using absorbing Markov chains in R. The attack is modeled as a set of transient stages and permanent absorbing outcomes. Using the Fundamental Matrix framework, we compute, for an assumed transition matrix, the closed-form probability that an attack ends in containment versus data exfiltration or ransomware, and the expected time to resolution. The goal is to illustrate how such a model can support discussion of detection and response priorities. It is not a validated risk quantification: the inputs are illustrative (see Parameterization and Assumptions). The term “attack graph” is used loosely here: the states are tactic-level stages, not the host, privilege, and vulnerability nodes of a formal attack graph.

The window shortens with depth. Expected time to resolution falls from 14.2 hours at S1 to 4.2 hours at S6, a decline of 70%. This is the time to any resolution; it shrinks partly because fewer stages remain. The time scale rests on the assumed 4-hour step.

Moving from the baseline to the illustrative improved posture raises containment by 24.8 to 40.5 percentage points depending on the starting stage, with the largest uplifts at S3 and S4 (39.9 and 40.5 pp). Because all rows change together, this does not identify which stage’s control matters most; see the one-row-at-a-time table.

Response targets such as MTTD under 4 hours and MTTR under 8 hours on initial endpoint compromises are consistent with this picture of neutralizing activity before S3: Privilege Escalation, but they follow from the assumed 4-hour step, not from the model, and should be set from observed dwell times.
Insight 2 (Active Directory Tier-0 Isolation): If an adversary reaches S5: Domain Dominance, the baseline probability of a catastrophic outcome is 80.7% (90% parameter-uncertainty interval 71.0%–89.1%). Under these parameters that supports prioritizing segregation of identity infrastructure; the figure is a function of the assumed S5 row, not a measured rate.
Insight 3 (Control Prioritization): Moving to the illustrative improved posture raises containment for an attack starting at S1 from 72.5% to 97.3% (+24.8 pp). Hardening one row at a time, the S1 and S2 rows carry the most leverage for attacks starting at S1. S2 ranks first in 61.9% of parameter draws and S1 in 31.6%, so their order is not robust. The size of the decline for deeper rows also depends on how the perturbation is defined: about 1.6× under a fixed 0.05 shift versus 4.0× under a proportional change. This illustrates how a control improvement translates into outcome probabilities; investment decisions require cost and loss inputs that this model does not contain.

text:
Insights & Conclusions
This project illustrates how an attack progression can be represented as an absorbing Markov chain and solved in closed form. Six kill-chain-style stages lead to three outcomes. For an assumed transition matrix, the Fundamental Matrix and matrix powers give the outcome probabilities, expected times, and full time-to-outcome distributions from every starting stage, without simulation. Under the illustrative baseline, an attack starting at S1 ends in a catastrophic outcome with probability 27.5%; when it does, it arrives in 25.0 hours on average and never before 16 hours. At the point estimate, catastrophic outcomes become more likely than containment at S3 (52.9% versus 47.1%). However, the crossing falls at S3 in only 38.0%–79.1% of parameter draws, depending on the assumed concentration α. The closed form is exact given \(P\), but \(P\) is uncertain, and the time layer in particular restates the 4-hour step assumption.
On where to act, the evidence is more limited than a comparison across starting stages suggests. The one-row-at-a-time analysis points to the S1 and S2 rows as carrying the most leverage for attacks starting at S1. Their order is not robust (S2 ranks first in 61.9% of draws), and the size of the decline for deeper rows depends on how a control change is represented. The paired comparison puts the illustrative improved posture’s containment uplift from S1 at 24.6 pp, with a 90% interval of 18.2 pp–31.7 pp. That is a scenario difference, not a measured control effect. Whether any real control (MFA, EDR, Zero Trust) corresponds to these parameter changes is not something this model can establish: there are no costs, loss magnitudes, or control-to-parameter mapping. Loss quantification, including any Cyber Value-at-Risk (CyVaR) figure, would need a stated loss mapping that is not part of this version.
Closed-form algebra replaces simulation for absorption probabilities, expected times, and time-to-outcome distributions. Monte Carlo is still needed to propagate parameter uncertainty; the simulation check reproduces \(B\), \(\mathbf{t}\), the conditional times, and one cumulative-incidence point as a correctness test. Other limitations are listed under Parameterization and Assumptions: the memoryless property, constant per-step hazard, geometric holding times, a single assumed step length coupled to the transition probabilities, a containment share that falls with depth by assumption, phishing as the only entry vector, permanent containment, mutually exclusive A2/A3 outcomes, and hand-set probabilities that are not calibrated to any cited benchmark. The natural next version is a continuous-time chain with stage-specific rates, which removes the time floor and lets controls act as hazard ratios. Real attackers adapt, and real environments differ.

title: The Model
text:
By organizing all attack states into a standardized matrix, the model separates transient stages (where the attacker is actively maneuvering) from absorbing states (permanent outcomes). Through closed-form matrix inversion, it computes the expected time spent in each stage and the probability of each terminal outcome, conditional on the assumed transition matrix.


Let the state space contain \(t\) transient states and \(r\) absorbing states (\(n = t + r\)). The transition probability matrix \(P \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}\) is partitioned into canonical block form:
\[P = \begin{pmatrix} Q & R \\ \mathbf{0} & I_r \end{pmatrix}\]

\(Q \in \mathbb{R}^{t \times t}\): Transition probabilities between transient states.
\(R \in \mathbb{R}^{t \times r}\): Transition probabilities from transient states into absorbing states.
\(\mathbf{0} \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times t}\): Zero matrix (absorbing states cannot transition back to transient states).
\(I_r \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times r}\): Identity matrix of order \(r\) (absorbing states are permanent).





If every transient state can reach an absorbing state, \((I_t - Q)\) is invertible. The Fundamental Matrix \(N \in \mathbb{R}^{t \times t}\) is:
\[N = (I_t - Q)^{-1} = I_t + Q + Q^2 + Q^3 + \dots = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} Q^k\]
Each entry \(N_{ij}\) is the expected number of time steps spent in transient state \(j\), given that the attack starts in transient state \(i\). Because \(N = I + Q + \dots\), the starting step counts: \(N_{ii} \ge 1\).




The expected number of steps before the chain is absorbed, from any starting state, is
\[\mathbf{t} = N \mathbf{1}, \qquad t_i = \sum_{j=1}^t N_{ij}\]
This is the expected time to resolution of any kind, including containment. A shorter time to resolution can mean faster containment (good) or faster detonation (bad), so it is not by itself a measure of adversary dwell. Each stage \(j\) has its own mean step duration \(h_j\) (hours), giving
\[\mathbf{T} = N \mathbf{h}\]
In this document every \(h_j = \Delta\tau = 4\) hours, so \(\mathbf{T} = 4\,\mathbf{t}\). The 4-hour step is an assumption. Rescaling hours to a different step is not a valid sensitivity check, because per-step probabilities only have meaning for the step length they were elicited for: a 1-hour step with the same \(P\) would imply a SOC that contains attacks four times faster per hour. A continuous-time formulation (rates per hour) removes this coupling.
The two layers of the model separate cleanly. The absorption probabilities \(B\) depend only on the embedded jump chain, meaning each transient row with its self-loop removed and the remaining entries renormalized. The self-loops and \(\Delta\tau\) affect timing only. The code below verifies this.




The matrix \(B \in \mathbb{R}^{t \times r}\) gives the probability that an attack starting in transient state \(i\) ends in absorbing state \(k\):
\[B = N R, \qquad \sum_{k=1}^r B_{ik} = 1 \;\; \text{for all } i\]




The expected time to resolution, conditional on ending in outcome \(k\), has the closed form
\[E[T \mid \text{start } i,\ \text{absorbed in } k] = \frac{\left(N\,(\mathbf{h} \circ B_{\cdot k})\right)_i}{B_{ik}}\]
where \(\circ\) is the elementwise product. For a catastrophic outcome, \(B_{\cdot k}\) is replaced by \(B_{\cdot A2} + B_{\cdot A3}\). This is the time metric that bears on response timelines, because it separates “time until containment” from “time until a catastrophic outcome, given that one occurs.”

title: The Model
text:
Parameterization and Assumptions
The model has six transient states (kill-chain-style stages) and three absorbing states (outcomes). Transition probabilities are expert-elicited, illustrative values. They are not calibrated to any cited benchmark, and they were typed in by hand: no asset graph, PageRank, CVSS weighting, or loss distribution is computed. Each transient row gives the per-step probability, from a given stage, of staying (self-loop), advancing, regressing, or ending in an absorbing outcome. The baseline and the improved-posture matrices are two hand-set matrices; the improved posture is not derived from any specific control (MFA, EDR, or Zero Trust).
Assumptions that the results depend on:

Markov property. “Starting at \(S_i\)” and “having reached \(S_i\)” are treated as identical, and the per-step detection hazard is constant. An attacker who reached \(S_3\) after 30 hours of slow movement has the same future as one who arrived in 4 hours; real detection probability can build up with time and noise.
Geometric holding times and a single step length. Each stage has a geometric holding time with a step length of \(\Delta\tau = 4\) hours for all stages. Because the self-loops are small (0.05–0.15), an attacker leaves each stage after a single step 85–95% of the time. The model’s timing is therefore close to deterministic, and no catastrophic outcome can occur in under 16 hours (see Time-to-Outcome Distributions). Real stages differ by orders of magnitude, from sub-hour lateral movement to multi-week dwell, so the implied time scale is a hypothetical, not a benchmark. The per-step probabilities are tied to the 4-hour step, so changing the step without re-eliciting them is not a valid sensitivity check.
S1 entry event. S1 begins when a user engages with a phishing lure (opens a malicious attachment, follows a malicious link, or submits credentials), not when a message is delivered. Filtered and ignored messages are outside the model. Under the baseline, 72% of S1 attacks eventually reach S2 (0.65 / 0.90). That is plausible only for this engaged cohort and would be far too high for delivered messages. Time spent in S1 is time to resolution, not dwell time in the industry sense, because the adversary is not yet inside the environment.
Outcome space. “Contained / Terminated” (A1) includes automated filtering, user non-engagement, abandoned attacks, and SOC action; it should not be read as “SOC wins.” A2 and A3 are mutually exclusive here, although double extortion (exfiltrate, then encrypt) is common; “catastrophic” counts only the first catastrophic outcome, and the A2/A3 split is not meaningful by itself. A1 is also treated as permanent, although containment is often partial and adversaries can re-enter through persistence or harvested credentials, so containment probabilities are upper bounds on durable containment.
Graph structure. Only S5 and S6 can reach A2/A3, and S6 has no regression edge, so catastrophic probability is largely P(reach S5/S6) times the S5/S6 exit split. The single back-edge S4 → S3 (0.05) is an illustrative attacker-backtracking edge with no empirical basis, kept in both regimes. The zeros from S2–S4 into A2 are also a strong claim: data theft from file shares or SaaS does not require domain dominance.
Containment share by depth. Conditional on leaving a stage, the share of exits that go to A1 falls from about 0.28–0.29 at S1–S2 to about 0.10–0.11 at S5–S6. That encodes a claim that defenders get worse at stopping attacks as the attacks become noisier. Deep stages usually generate the richest telemetry; what shrinks is the time left to respond. A continuous-time formulation, in which detection and progression are competing rates, can reproduce falling containment at depth without this assumption.
Single entry vector. Phishing is the only way in. Exploits were the most common initial infection vector in Mandiant’s 2024 investigations, at 33% (M-Trends 2025). In 56% of Sophos’s 2024 cases, adversaries logged in with valid credentials rather than breaking in (Sophos). Valid-credential entry would skip S1 and start at S2 or S3.



Display code
# Build a 9x9 transition matrix from the rows listed in params.yaml
matrix_from_params <- function(rows, transient, absorbing) {
  all_states <- c(transient, absorbing)
  stopifnot(length(rows) == length(transient), all(lengths(rows) == length(all_states)))
  P <- matrix(0, length(all_states), length(all_states), dimnames = list(all_states, all_states))
  P[transient, ] <- do.call(rbind, map(rows, unlist))
  P[absorbing, absorbing] <- diag(length(absorbing))
  P
}
transient_names <- params$states$transient
absorbing_names <- params$states$absorbing
all_state_names <- c(transient_names, absorbing_names)
t_dim <- length(transient_names)
r_dim <- length(absorbing_names)

# Mean step duration per transient stage (hours); the same for every stage by assumption
step_hours <- setNames(rep(params$step_hours$value, t_dim), transient_names)

# Baseline and improved-posture transition matrices P (9x9), illustrative values from params.yaml
P_baseline_raw <- matrix_from_params(params$transition_matrices$baseline, transient_names, absorbing_names)
P_hardened_raw <- matrix_from_params(params$transition_matrices$improved, transient_names, absorbing_names)

# Every row must be a probability distribution
stopifnot(all(abs(rowSums(P_baseline_raw) - 1) < 1e-8))
stopifnot(all(abs(rowSums(P_hardened_raw) - 1) < 1e-8))

Q_base <- P_baseline_raw[1:t_dim, 1:t_dim]
R_base <- P_baseline_raw[1:t_dim, (t_dim + 1):(t_dim + r_dim)]
Q_hard <- P_hardened_raw[1:t_dim, 1:t_dim]
R_hard <- P_hardened_raw[1:t_dim, (t_dim + 1):(t_dim + r_dim)]

section: Pure R Algebraic Solver: Fundamental Matrix & Time to Resolution
text:
Pure R Algebraic Solver: Fundamental Matrix & Time to Resolution
The solver computes \(N\), expected time to resolution, absorption probabilities, and conditional times to each outcome. Before inverting, it checks that every transient state can reach an absorbing state (which guarantees \(I - Q\) is invertible) and, after computing \(B\), that every row of \(B\) sums to 1.


Display code
# TRUE if every transient state has a path to an absorbing state
all_reach_absorbing <- function(Q, R) {
  reach <- rowSums(R) > 0
  repeat {
    updated <- reach | as.vector((Q > 0) %*% reach) > 0
    if (identical(updated, reach)) break
    reach <- updated
  }
  all(reach)
}

solve_absorbing_markov <- function(Q, R, h) {
  stopifnot(all_reach_absorbing(Q, R))

  N <- solve(diag(nrow(Q)) - Q, tol = 1e-14)
  dimnames(N) <- dimnames(Q)

  B <- N %*% R
  stopifnot(all(abs(rowSums(B) - 1) < 1e-8))

  # Conditional expected time to each outcome: N (h * B_k) / B_k
  time_given_outcome <- apply(B, 2, \(b) as.vector(N %*% (h * b)) / b)
  rownames(time_given_outcome) <- rownames(Q)

  cat_prob <- B[, 2] + B[, 3]
  time_given_catastrophe <- as.vector(N %*% (h * cat_prob)) / cat_prob

  list(
    N = N,
    B = B,
    steps = rowSums(N),
    hours = as.vector(N %*% h) |> setNames(rownames(Q)),
    time_given_outcome = time_given_outcome,
    time_given_catastrophe = setNames(time_given_catastrophe, rownames(Q))
  )
}
base_solution <- solve_absorbing_markov(Q_base, R_base, step_hours)
hard_solution <- solve_absorbing_markov(Q_hard, R_hard, step_hours)




Display code
# B depends only on the embedded jump chain: remove self-loops and renormalize
jump_chain <- function(P) {
  for (i in seq_len(t_dim)) {
    s <- P[i, i]
    P[i, i] <- 0
    P[i, ] <- P[i, ] / (1 - s)
  }
  P
}
J_base <- jump_chain(P_baseline_raw)
B_jump <- solve_absorbing_markov(
  J_base[1:t_dim, 1:t_dim], J_base[1:t_dim, (t_dim + 1):(t_dim + r_dim)], step_hours
)$B
stopifnot(max(abs(B_jump - base_solution$B)) < 1e-10)

# Depth diagnostics used in the text
holding_steps_b <- 1 / (1 - diag(Q_base))
p_leave_first_step <- 1 - diag(Q_base)
a1_share_b <- P_baseline_raw[1:t_dim, t_dim + 1] / (1 - diag(Q_base))
a1_share_h <- P_hardened_raw[1:t_dim, t_dim + 1] / (1 - diag(Q_hard))
stopifnot(round(range(a1_share_b), 2) == c(0.11, 0.29))

# One row per starting stage; prose numbers on every page are drawn from this table
res <- tibble(
  stage = transient_names,
  steps_b = base_solution$steps,
  hours_b = base_solution$hours,

title: The Model
text:
Diagnostic Visualizations & Outcome Decomposition
The diagnostic plots below show the routing structure of the transition matrix, the expected time to resolution from each starting stage, the conditional time to each outcome, the baseline absorption probabilities, and the change in catastrophic probability under the improved posture.


The Transition Probability Matrix (P) plot
The heatmap shows the main paths an intrusion can take under the assumed parameters and where the per-step exit probabilities sit.


Display code
matrix_df <- as.data.frame(P_baseline_raw) |>
  rownames_to_column(var = "From_State") |>
  pivot_longer(cols = -From_State, names_to = "To_State", values_to = "Probability") |>
  mutate(
    Fill_Prob = if_else(From_State %in% absorbing_names, NA_real_, Probability),
    From_State = factor(From_State, levels = rev(all_state_names)),
    To_State = factor(To_State, levels = all_state_names)
  )

p1_heatmap <- ggplot(matrix_df, aes(x = To_State, y = From_State, fill = Fill_Prob)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_text(aes(label = ifelse(Probability > 0, sprintf("%.2f", Probability), "")), size = 3.2) +
  scale_fill_gradient(
    low = "#f8f9fa", high = "#d9534f",
    limits = c(0, max(P_baseline_raw[1:t_dim, ])),
    na.value = "#e9ecef", name = "P(Transition)"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Kill-Chain Transition Probability Matrix (P)",
    subtitle = "Illustrative baseline; absorbing rows (identity) shown in gray and excluded from the color scale",
    x = "Target State (t + 1)",
    y = "Origin State (t)"
  ) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, size = 8.5),
        axis.text.y = element_text(size = 8.5))

p1_heatmap









How to read the plot. Each row is where an attacker is now, and each column is where they can be one 4-hour step later. The number in a cell is the assumed chance of that move, and darker red means more likely; each row adds up to 1. The first six columns are attack stages, A1 is containment, and A2 and A3 are data theft and ransomware. The gray rows at the bottom are final outcomes, which never change once reached.
What the plot tells you. Most of the weight sits just right of the diagonal, so an attacker who is not stopped usually moves one stage deeper at each step. The chance of containment in a single step falls from 0.25 at the first stage to 0.10 at the last, and catastrophic outcomes are possible only from the last two stages. These numbers are assumed inputs, not measurements, and every other result on this site follows from them.
In more detail
Directional momentum. The super-diagonal carries the largest transient-to-transient probabilities (0.65 from S1 to S2, 0.55 S2 to S3, 0.60 S3 to S4, 0.55 S4 to S5, 0.70 S5 to S6), so under these parameters an attack that is not stopped keeps advancing.
Per-step exit probabilities to A1. The per-step probability of ending in \(A_1\) is 0.25 at S1 and 0.25 at S2, and falls to 0.10 at S6, where the per-step catastrophic probability is 0.85. These are assumed inputs, not findings, so they cannot by themselves show where defensive investment pays off most; the one-row-at-a-time analysis on the Robustness page addresses that question.
Containment share falls with depth by assumption. Conditional on leaving a stage, the probability that the exit is A1 is 0.28, 0.29, 0.22, 0.18, 0.11, 0.11 for S1 through S6 under the baseline, and 0.58, 0.56, 0.53, 0.44, 0.37, 0.37 under the improved posture. This encodes a claim that defenders get worse at stopping attacks as they become noisier. In practice, lateral movement, credential access, and payload staging generate the richest telemetry; what shrinks at depth is the time left to respond, not necessarily the probability of detection.



The Expected Time to Resolution Plot
The expected time to resolution is the expected time until the incident ends in any outcome, including containment. It is not adversary dwell time: a shorter value can reflect faster containment or faster detonation.


Display code
ttr_df <- res |>
  select(Origin_State = stage, Baseline = hours_b, Improved = hours_h) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = c(Baseline, Improved), names_to = "Architecture", values_to = "Hours") |>
  mutate(
    Origin_State = factor(Origin_State, levels = transient_names),
    Architecture = recode(Architecture,
      Baseline = "Baseline (illustrative)",
      Improved = "Improved posture (illustrative)"
    )
  )

p2_ttr <- ggplot(ttr_df, aes(x = Origin_State, y = Hours, fill = Architecture)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1fh", Hours)), position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), vjust = -0.4, size = 3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Baseline (illustrative)" = "#d9534f", "Improved posture (illustrative)" = "#0275d8")) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  labs(
    title = "Expected Time to Resolution",
    subtitle = "Expected steps to any terminal outcome from each starting stage, times an assumed 4-hour step",
    x = "Attack Origin State",
    y = "Expected Hours (4h / Step)"
  ) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 35, hjust = 1, size = 8.5))

p2_ttr









How to read the plot. Each pair of bars is a starting stage, from S1 on the left to S6 on the right. The height of a bar is the expected number of hours until the incident ends in any way, whether contained or catastrophic. Red bars are the baseline and blue bars the improved posture, and the label on each bar gives its value. Hours are the expected number of steps multiplied by the assumed 4 hours per step.
What the plot tells you. Incidents end sooner the deeper the attack starts: under the baseline, 14.2 hours from S1 against 4.2 hours from S6, partly because fewer stages remain. The improved posture ends incidents sooner, mainly by containing them earlier. A shorter time is not automatically good news, though: it can mean faster containment or a faster catastrophe, and this plot cannot tell the two apart.
In more detail
Time to resolution shortens with depth. Under the baseline, expected time to resolution falls from 3.5 steps (14.2 hours) for an attack starting at S1 to 1.1 steps (4.2 hours) at S6. Part of this is mechanical, since there are fewer stages left to traverse; part is outcome mix.
The improved posture shortens it mainly through earlier containment. From S1 through S3 the improved posture lowers the expected time to resolution from 12.6–14.2 hours to 7.6–7.9 hours, but the plot cannot separate faster containment (good) from faster detonation (bad); the conditional times below can.
The S6 values are identical by construction. The baseline and improved S6 rows share the same self-loop (0.05), so S6 shows 4.2 hours in both regimes. This is a parameter choice, not a finding about late-stage defense.



Conditional Time to Containment versus Time to a Catastrophic Outcome

  labs(
    title = "Expected Time to Outcome, Conditional on That Outcome",
    subtitle = "E[T | start i, absorbed in outcome], assuming a 4-hour step",
    x = "Attack Origin State",
    y = "Expected Hours"
  ) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, size = 8))

p_cond









How to read the plot. Each pair of bars is a starting stage, and the two panels compare the baseline with the improved posture. The green bar is the expected time until the attack is contained, counting only attacks that end contained. The red bar is the expected time until data theft or ransomware, counting only attacks that end that way. Times are in hours at an assumed 4 hours per step, and the labels give each value.
What the plot tells you. Containment, when it happens, comes sooner than catastrophe: from S1 under the baseline, 10.1 hours against 25.0 hours. The red bars matter most for a response plan, because they show roughly how long defenders have before an unstopped attack does serious damage. They shrink with depth, to 4.2 hours at S6. The hours follow from the assumed step length, not from observed attacks.
In more detail. Conditional on ending in a catastrophic outcome, the baseline expected time to that outcome is 25.0 hours from S1, versus 10.1 hours to containment. The metric that bears on a response timeline is the first: under these assumptions, an attack that starts at phishing delivery and goes on to a catastrophic outcome takes about 25 hours to get there. This figure scales linearly with the assumed 4-hour step and rests on the memoryless assumption.



Time-to-Outcome Distributions and the Structural Floor
Means hide the shape of the timing. The cumulative incidence function (CIF) for outcome \(k\), starting from stage \(i\), is the probability that the attack has ended in \(k\) by step \(s\):
\[\mathrm{CIF}_k(s) = \sum_{u=0}^{s-1} \mathbf{e}_i^\top Q^u R_{\cdot k}\]
It is exact in closed form from matrix powers, with no simulation needed.


Display code
# Probability of absorption into each outcome at each step, by matrix powers
outcome_pmf <- function(Q, R, start = 1, max_steps = 200) {
  x <- replace(numeric(nrow(Q)), start, 1)
  out <- matrix(0, max_steps, ncol(R), dimnames = list(NULL, colnames(R)))
  for (s in seq_len(max_steps)) {
    out[s, ] <- as.vector(x %*% R)
    x <- as.vector(x %*% Q)
  }
  out
}
stopifnot(length(unique(step_hours)) == 1)

pmf_b <- outcome_pmf(Q_base, R_base, start = 1)
pmf_h <- outcome_pmf(Q_hard, R_hard, start = 1)
hours_grid <- seq_len(nrow(pmf_b)) * unname(step_hours[1])

cat_pmf_b <- pmf_b[, 2] + pmf_b[, 3]
cond_cat_b <- cat_pmf_b / sum(cat_pmf_b)
cond_cont_b <- pmf_b[, 1] / sum(pmf_b[, 1])
q_at <- function(cond, p) hours_grid[which(cumsum(cond) >= p - 1e-12)[1]]
q_cat_b <- map_dbl(c(0.10, 0.50, 0.90, 0.99), \(p) q_at(cond_cat_b, p))
q_cont_b <- map_dbl(c(0.50, 0.90), \(p) q_at(cond_cont_b, p))
floor_cat_h <- hours_grid[which(cat_pmf_b > 0)[1]]
mean_cat_b <- sum(hours_grid * cond_cat_b)
sd_cat_b <- sqrt(sum((hours_grid - mean_cat_b)^2 * cond_cat_b))
cov_cat_b <- sd_cat_b / mean_cat_b
p_cat_by_24h <- sum(cat_pmf_b[hours_grid <= 24])

# Consistency with the closed form, and guards for numbers quoted as static text
stopifnot(abs(mean_cat_b - res$t_cat_b[1]) < 1e-6)
stopifnot(abs(sum(pmf_b) - 1) < 1e-8)
stopifnot(floor_cat_h == 16, round(res$t_cat_b[1], 1) == 25.0)




Display code
cif_df <- bind_rows(
  tibble(Regime = "Baseline", Hours = hours_grid,
         Contained = cumsum(pmf_b[, 1]), Catastrophic = cumsum(pmf_b[, 2] + pmf_b[, 3])),
  tibble(Regime = "Improved posture", Hours = hours_grid,
         Contained = cumsum(pmf_h[, 1]), Catastrophic = cumsum(pmf_h[, 2] + pmf_h[, 3]))
) |>
  bind_rows(tibble(Regime = c("Baseline", "Improved posture"), Hours = 0, Contained = 0, Catastrophic = 0)) |>
  pivot_longer(c(Contained, Catastrophic), names_to = "Outcome", values_to = "CIF") |>
  filter(Hours <= 60) |>
  arrange(Regime, Outcome, Hours)

p_cif <- ggplot(cif_df, aes(x = Hours, y = CIF, color = Outcome)) +
  geom_step(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = floor_cat_h, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray40") +
  facet_wrap(~Regime) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Contained = "#5cb85c", Catastrophic = "#d9534f")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(), limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 60, 8)) +
  labs(
    title = "Cumulative Incidence of Each Outcome, Attack Starting at S1",
    subtitle = sprintf("P(outcome reached by hour t); dashed line = structural floor of %d h for any catastrophic outcome (4-hour step)", floor_cat_h),
    x = "Hours since start (4-hour steps)",
    y = "Cumulative incidence"
  )

p_cif









How to read the plot. Each line shows, for an attack that starts at S1, the chance that it has ended in a given way by a given hour. The green line is containment and the red line a catastrophic outcome (data theft or ransomware); the left panel is the baseline and the right the improved posture. The lines climb in steps because the model moves in 4-hour steps. The dashed line marks hour 16.
What the plot tells you. No catastrophic outcome can happen before hour 16, because the shortest route to one takes four 4-hour steps; this floor comes from the model’s design, not from attacker behavior. Under the baseline, the chance of catastrophe reaches 17.9% by hour 24 and levels off at 27.5%. Under the improved posture it levels off at only 2.7%. Real attacks can move much faster or slower than this fixed schedule allows.
In more detail
A hard floor. The chain moves one edge per 4-hour step, and the shortest path to a catastrophic outcome from S1 (S1 → S2 → S4 → S6 → A3) has four edges. No catastrophic outcome can therefore occur before 16 hours. By 24 hours, the probability of a catastrophic outcome is 17.9%, out of a lifetime 27.5%.
An almost fixed schedule. Conditional on a catastrophic outcome, the 10th, 50th, 90th, and 99th percentiles of time from S1 are 20, 24, 32, 40 hours, with a coefficient of variation of 0.19. Conditional on containment, the median and 90th percentile are 8 and 20 hours. Each stage is left after one step 85.0%–95.0% of the time, so time to catastrophe is close to (number of stages traversed) × 4 hours.
Benchmarks fall outside this range on both sides. The average eCrime breakout time, from the first compromised host to another, was 48 minutes in 2024 (CrowdStrike 2025 Global Threat Report). Sophos reports a median of 11 hours from an attacker’s initial action to the first attempt on Active Directory (Sophos 2025 Active Adversary Report). Mandiant reports a 2024 median dwell time of 11 days overall and 6 days for ransomware intrusions (M-Trends 2025). The discrete 4-hour chain can represent neither the sub-hour tail nor the multi-week tail, so its time outputs should be read as a restatement of the step assumption.



The Baseline Terminal Absorption Frontier Plot
The plot decomposes the final outcome of an attack by starting stage, under the baseline parameters.


Display code
absorb_df <- as.data.frame(base_solution$B) |>
  rownames_to_column(var = "Origin_State") |>
  pivot_longer(cols = -Origin_State, names_to = "Absorbing_Outcome", values_to = "Probability") |>
  mutate(
    Origin_State = factor(Origin_State, levels = transient_names),
    Absorbing_Outcome = factor(Absorbing_Outcome, levels = absorbing_names)
  )

p3_frontier <- ggplot(absorb_df, aes(x = Origin_State, y = Probability, fill = Absorbing_Outcome)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f%%", Probability * 100)),
            position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5), size = 3.2, color = "white", fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = setNames(c("#5cb85c", "#f0ad4e", "#d9534f"), absorbing_names)
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format()) +
  labs(
    title = "Baseline Terminal Absorption Frontier",
    subtitle = "Decomposition of final incident outcomes by starting stage (illustrative parameters)",
    x = "Attack Origin State",
    y = "Absorption Probability (%)",
    fill = "Terminal State"
  ) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 35, hjust = 1, size = 8.5))

p3_frontier









How to read the plot. Each bar is a starting stage, and its colored segments show how attacks starting there end under the baseline. Green is containment, orange is data exfiltration, and red is ransomware. Each bar adds up to 100%, and the labels give each share. Reading from left to right shows how the final outcome changes the deeper into the network an attack starts. These are shares across many hypothetical attacks, not a forecast for any single incident.
What the plot tells you. The deeper the starting point, the worse the outcome. Containment falls from 72.5% at S1 to 10.5% at S6, and at S3, privilege escalation, a catastrophic outcome (52.9%) first becomes more likely than containment. That makes S3 the model’s tipping point, although the uncertainty analysis shows the exact stage is not certain. The split between data theft and ransomware is itself an assumption.
In more detail
Containment declines with depth. Under the baseline parameters, the probability of ending in \(A_1\) falls from 72.5% for an attack starting at S1 to 47.1% at S3, where catastrophic outcomes (52.9%) first become more likely than containment. This crossing follows directly from the hand-set S2 and S3 rows; the uncertainty analysis on the Robustness page shows how stable it is.
Catastrophic probability rises steeply. Combined catastrophic probability (A2 plus A3) grows from 27.5% at S1 to 80.7% at S5 and 89.5% at S6.
The A2/A3 split should not be over-read. At S5 and S6 the split is roughly even (A2 38.3%–42.1%, A3 42.4%–47.4%), but A2 and A3 are modeled as mutually exclusive, whereas double extortion is common in practice. In the improved-posture matrix, A2 equals A3 at S5 and S6 because the two columns were assigned identical values, which shows the split is a parameter choice.



The Catastrophic Breach Risk Under an Improved Posture
The plot contrasts baseline catastrophic probability with the illustrative improved posture. The improved-posture matrix changes all six rows at once, so differences across starting stages reflect where the attacker begins, not where a control is applied.


Display code
comparison_df <- res |>
  transmute(
    Origin_State = factor(stage, levels = transient_names),
    Baseline_Catastrophic = cat_b * 100,
    Hardened_Catastrophic = cat_h * 100
  )

p4_reduction <- ggplot(comparison_df, aes(x = Origin_State)) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = Origin_State, y = Hardened_Catastrophic, yend = Baseline_Catastrophic),
               color = "gray60", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(aes(y = Baseline_Catastrophic, color = "Baseline"), size = 3.5) +
  geom_point(aes(y = Hardened_Catastrophic, color = "Improved posture"), size = 3.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Baseline" = "#d9534f", "Improved posture" = "#0275d8"), name = "Posture") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%")) +
  labs(
    title = "Catastrophic Breach Probability: Baseline vs. Improved Posture",
    subtitle = "Probability of terminal ransomware or exfiltration, by starting stage (illustrative parameters)",
    x = "Attack Origin State",
    y = "Combined Catastrophic Probability (%)"
  ) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 35, hjust = 1, size = 8.5))

p4_reduction









How to read the plot. Each column is a starting stage. The red dot is the chance that an attack starting there ends in data theft or ransomware under the baseline, and the blue dot is the same chance under the improved posture. The gray line between them shows the size of the reduction, so a shorter line means a smaller benefit at that stage. The vertical axis is in percent, and both postures use the same illustrative model.
What the plot tells you. The improved posture lowers the chance of catastrophe from every starting stage, by 24.8 to 40.5 percentage points. Residual risk is lowest from S1, at 2.7%, but that is partly built in: an attack starting at S1 must pass through all six improved stages. Residual risk is highest from S6, at 63.2%. The plot therefore does not show where to invest; the one-row-at-a-time analysis addresses that.
In more detail
Lower catastrophic probability at every stage. By construction, the improved posture (blue) lowers combined catastrophic probability relative to the baseline (red) from every starting stage.
Where the absolute reductions are largest. The reductions in catastrophic probability are 24.8, 31.6, 39.9, 40.5, 36.9, 26.3 percentage points for S1 through S6. The largest absolute reductions occur at S4: Lateral Movement and S3: Privilege Escalation.
Why S1 shows the lowest residual risk. From S1 the catastrophic probability falls from 27.5% to 2.7%, versus 89.5% to 63.2% from S6. This is guaranteed by the setup: an attacker starting at S1 passes through all six hardened rows, one starting at S6 only through the last. It is not evidence that upstream investment has greater leverage. The one-row-at-a-time analysis on the Robustness page tests that question directly.

title: Reproducibility
text: Every number on this site is computed at render time from the parameters in params.yaml. No data are downloaded or read from elsewhere, every random draw is seeded, and package versions are pinned with renv, so rendering the same commit gives the same results. This page explains how to rerun the analysis, how the scripts fit together, what the tests check, and records the software environment.

title: Reproducibility
text:
Quick start

The code and data are in the GitHub repository patrick-lefler/attack-graph-simulation-via-markov-chains. You need R 4.3 or later and Quarto 1.5 or later. To rebuild the results, run the tests and render the site from a clean copy:
Restore the packages with renv::restore() (see Software environment).
Rebuild everything from the project root:

Rscript run_all.R
run_all.R checks that the installed packages match renv.lock, runs the tests, and then re-executes and renders every page into docs/. It stops at the first problem. To run the analysis in an R console without rendering, source the scripts in order from the project root:
source("R/00_setup.R")
source("R/01_model.R")
source("R/02_robustness.R")
Each script depends on objects and packages from the one before it, so sourcing a later script on its own in a fresh session fails. The full analysis takes about 20 seconds.

title: Reproducibility
text:
Parameters and seeds
All parameters live in params.yaml. Each is labelled as an assumption (an illustrative or elicited value with no empirical source) or a design choice (a simulation or perturbation size that affects precision or framing, not the model), with the range the analysis explores. Several numbers derived from these values are quoted as fixed text on the site, and stopifnot() guards in R/01_model.R stop the render if a parameter change breaks one, so the text must be updated along with the value.
Every random stream is seeded explicitly with the seed value (42): once in R/00_setup.R and again at the start of each random section of R/02_robustness.R. Each section therefore gives the same draws regardless of which sections run before it. The closed-form solver itself is deterministic. The full file:

How to read the table. Each row is one test, grouped by the file it lives in: parameters, solver, model, and the functions used in the robustness analysis. The Checks column counts the individual comparisons inside the test, and Result shows whether every one of them passed. The solver tests compare the code against a two-stage chain small enough to solve by hand, so they check the arithmetic against an independent answer.
What the table tells you. Every test passed in this render. The tests check that the code does what it describes. They cannot check whether the illustrative transition probabilities are realistic. If a later change breaks one of these properties, run_all.R stops before rendering any page, and the failing row names the test.

title: Reproducibility
text:
Caching

No results cache. The full analysis runs in about 20 seconds, so every page recomputes it when rendered.
Quarto freeze (_freeze/). _quarto.yml sets freeze: auto, so a full quarto render re-executes a page only when that page’s .qmd file changes. Edits to params.yaml or the R/ scripts do not count as a change. After editing either, run Rscript run_all.R, which renders each page explicitly, because Quarto always executes a page that is rendered on its own.
